chunks: My father (RA) said: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Marwan ibn Ubayd, from 'Amr, one of our scholars, from the one who asked Abu Abd Allah (AS):

He said to him: 'I have a family member who belongs to the Qadariya and who says: We are able to do so and so, and we are able not to do so.' He said: Abu Abd Allah (AS) said: 'Tell him: Do you have the ability to remember what you abhor, and to forget what you like?' If he says: 'No,' then he has denounced his statement, and if he says: 'Yes,' then do not speak to him again, for he has claimed to be God.

key_terms.أَصْحَابِنَا: Our scholars/companions (referring to the Shia scholars)
key_terms.قَدَرِيَّةٌ: Qadariya (a theological sect emphasizing human free will and ability)

ai.seo_question: How does the Imam test the Qadariya's claim of human capability?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq employs this logical test to refute the Qadariya's claim of absolute human autonomy (Istita'ah Mutlaqah) by highlighting the limitation of human will over involuntary mental processes like memory. In Shia theology, this serves as a bridge between human agency and divine omnipotence, demonstrating that if humans cannot even control their own cognition, they certainly cannot possess independent power over all actions. This nuanced view preserves human responsibility (Taklif) while affirming that ultimate capability is derived from God, avoiding the extremes of absolute determinism (Jabr) and absolute free will (Tafwid).
